title: U.S. Returns Old MQ-1 Predator Drones to Service After New MQ-9s Take Unsustainable Losses to Iran
body: The United States Air Force has returned the MQ-1 Predator drone to frontline service more than eight years after the type was officially retired, providing a remarkable revival for one of the most iconic combat drones of the post-Cold War era. This follows extreme losses to the MQ-9 Reaper fleet, with close to 60 Reapers having been shot down or destroyed on the ground by Iranian and allied Yemeni Ansuruallah Coalition forces, the large majority of them since February 2026, leaving the U.S. Air Force unable to sustain operations. The scale of the losses has made the availability of lower-cost unmanned aircraft increasingly important, with the Predator’s status as a previously retired aircraft making it largely expendable. Iran has repeatedly claimed that American MQ-1 aircraft have been destroyed during the conflict. On September 21, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps stated that it had intercepted a U.S. MQ-1 over the Strait of Hormuz using a new air- defence system. The MQ-9 is considerably larger and more expensive than the original Predator, while its sophisticated sensors and communications equipment make each loss particularly consequential. It remains uncertain how many Predators may have been lost in combat, however, as some MQ-1s reported destroyed appear to have been new and much more valuable MQ-1C Gray Eagles rather than old MQ-1 Predators. The revival of the Predator illustrates the changing economics of unmanned warfare. The original MQ-1 was designed around relatively simple and inexpensive persistent surveillance. It later became the first major U.S. armed unmanned aircraft, carrying AGM-114 Hellfire missiles in addition to electro-optical and infrared sensors. The MQ-9 Reaper was subsequently developed to provide substantially greater speed, payload and sensor capacity. Its larger airframe also allowed it to carry a considerably broader selection of weapons and equipment. Despite its superior capabilities, the Reaper’s far greater cost become a liability when deployed for high intensity operations. The Predator’s unexpected second life consequently highlights a broader feature of the current conflict: the value of quantity alongside sophistication. An older unmanned aircraft cannot replicate the capabilities of an MQ-9, but a relatively inexpensive platform can still provide useful surveillance or serve as a test and training asset without consuming the same resources as the newest generation of American unmanned systems. While Reaper drones have formed a vital part of the U.S. Air Force’s reconnaissance-strike complex, and have been flown into contested air space for intelligence gathering and in some cases for strike operations, relying on the Predator for such missions can help preserve the much more valuable Reaper fleet.

title: Russia fabricates Dobropillia encirclement to strengthen its case for Kyiv’s capitulation at UN – ISW
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed on 22 September 2026 that it had surrounded Dobropillia, but the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) found no evidence to support the announcement. Dobropillia is a small town in Donetsk Oblast, known as the "pearl of the Donbas" for its coal industry, which has helped make Ukraine's Fortress Belt cities, holding the region from Russians since 2014, per RBC Ukraine. Ukraine’s Vivaldi counteroffensive in Donetsk Oblast broke the northern arm of Russia’s plan to surround the fortified cities. ISW says Moscow’s Dobropillia claim diverts attention from that setback and portrays Ukrainian defenses as collapsing during the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, held on 21-28 September. The institute says Russia is likely spreading such claims to support its push for Ukraine’s capitulation. Meanwhile, Ukrainian officers say Russian assault groups are still trying to break through toward Dobropillia, but have made no major gains. Russia’s encirclement claim clashes with Ukrainian battlefield reports Russia’s Ministry of Defense has claimed its troops were advancing toward Oleksandrivka, a village northwest of Dobropillia, but published no map to support its account. At the same time, Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets said Ukrainian troops still held positions south and northeast of the city, which the experts said was inconsistent with the claimed encirclement. ISW reported that a Ukrainian artillery reconnaissance battalion chief of staff said on 22 September that Russia had made no major advances near Dobropillia. He said Russian commanders kept postponing deadlines because of heavy losses and a gap between their plans and battlefield conditions. A Ukrainian battalion officer said Russian troops were still trying to slip through Ukrainian lines in small groups. How Dobropillia fits Russia’s plan to surround the fortress belt Dobropillia is a transport hub on the southwestern approach to Ukraine’s “fortress belt,” which includes Kostiantynivka, Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk, and Sloviansk. These cities have anchored Ukraine’s defense in Donetsk Oblast since 2022. Ukraine’s Third Army Corps commander, Andrii Biletskyi, whose corps is conducting the Vivaldi counteroffensive north of Lyman, explained that Russian forces advancing through Dobropillia were meant to join another force coming from north of Lyman, behind the fortified cities, encircling them rather than attacking them head-on. Ukraine’s Third Army Corps commander, Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, announced “Operation Vivaldi” on 15 September 2026. Source: screenshot from Ukraine’s Third Army Corps announcement of Vivaldi ISW had already assessed on 16 September that Vivaldi had made the two-sided plan infeasible. In its 22 September report, ISW said Russia’s false claim about Dobropillia partly aims to divert attention from those Ukrainian gains. Russian assaults toward Dobropillia continue The setback north of Lyman has not stopped Russia’s push toward Dobropillia. Ukrainian staff sergeant Dmytro Davydenko reported on 14 September a sharp increase in assault groups moving toward the city, sometimes more than his unit could engage. He said Ukrainian troops had mined, blocked, or destroyed the main approaches. ISW reported that Russia was preparing armor and drone support for possible assaults using armored vehicles this fall. A Ukrainian battalion officer said fog might help Russia move that equipment, although Ukrainian reconnaissance and drones would make it difficult. He said Russian glide bombs continued to strike infrastructure in the area. title: B-2 Spirit stealth bombers demonstrate enduring strategic value for U.S. global-strike capability throughout Operation Epic Fury
body: U.S. Central Command identified the B-2 among the aircraft employed during the operation’s first 72 hours, when American forces struck more than 1,700 targets. Military imagery subsequently documented B-2 activity on March 18 and April 2, followed by a confirmed combat departure from an undisclosed base in the U.S. Strategic Command area of responsibility on April 5. The operational pattern suggests the B-2 was used as a sustained combat asset rather than reserved for a single, highly choreographed opening strike. It also showed that the U.S. could continue generating stealth-bomber missions while a far larger regional air campaign placed heavy demands on aircraft, maintenance crews, tankers and weapons inventories. For commanders, the B-2 offers a combination that few other aircraft can match: intercontinental reach, a large weapons load and the ability to penetrate sophisticated air defenses. The bomber can fly approximately 6,000 nautical miles without refueling and carry about 40,000 pounds of conventional or nuclear weapons. Those characteristics gave Washington the option to strike high-value targets from bases outside the immediate theater, reducing its reliance on locations exposed to Iranian missiles and drones. They also allowed the United States to retain a manned penetrating-strike capability while fighters, carrier aircraft and non-stealth bombers handled other parts of the campaign. Publicly available information does not disclose how many B-2 sorties were flown, which targets were assigned to the aircraft or what weapons they delivered. The Pentagon has also not released platform-specific assessments showing how many targets the bombers destroyed, leaving their performance to be measured principally through their sustained operational use. The B-2 operated alongside B-1 Lancers and B-52 Stratofortresses in a bomber force supported by fighters, aerial-refueling tankers, surveillance aircraft and electronic-attack platforms. This mix allowed commanders to assign aircraft according to target defenses, range, payload requirements and the level of risk presented by each mission. By April 1, U.S. forces had struck more than 12,300 targets and completed more than 13,000 combat flights, illustrating the scale of the air operation in which the B-2 participated. The broader campaign ultimately included approximately 36,000 combat sorties, more than 1,800 fire missions and strikes against about 13,500 targets. The bomber’s performance carries broader significance for U.S. force planning because the Air Force is preparing to replace the B-2 and B-1 with the next-generation B-21 Raider. Operation Epic Fury provided a fresh demonstration of the military requirement the B-21 is intended to inherit: delivering conventional or nuclear weapons over intercontinental distances and penetrating contested airspace. The Lead Inspector General report to Congress on Operation Epic Fury said U.S. Strategic Command provided global-strike capabilities from the continental United States and forward bases throughout the campaign. It said those operations included dozens of 2,000-pound penetrating guided bombs dropped on deeply buried missile launchers across southern Iran during the first 11 days, although it did not attribute those strikes or their results specifically to the B-2.

title: Russia is mapping everyday targets across Kyiv, from trolleybus depots to Zhuliany airport, top monitoring channel says, ahead of next ballistic strike
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russia is scouting Kyiv and the surrounding region for its next targets, from power substations and railways to hypermarkets and airports. Nikolaievsky Vaniok, a major Ukrainian monitoring channel, says Russian aerial reconnaissance has been mapping specific sites across the capital and Kyiv Oblast, and a national-security official warns that a ballistic strike is being prepared. The reported scouting fits Russia's pattern of taking apart Ukraine's power and civilian infrastructure as winter nears, with Moscow switching to terror or rear as its tactics of the war. Signs of preparation are present Andrii Kovalenko, who heads the National Security Council's Center for Countering Disinformation, has also confirmed Russia is preparing a ballistic strike, with signs of the preparation visible, while its diplomats stall on any real step toward a ceasefire. Ballistics are the threat Ukraine's air defenses struggle most to stop: in a recent attack on Kyiv's water system, not one of Russia's ballistic missiles was intercepted. "The enemy is preparing a ballistic strike. Signs of preparation are present," he wrote, adding the warning to "be attentive in the coming days." The scouting maps the everyday Nikolaievsky Vaniok, which tracks Russian air activity, says the reconnaissance had lingered over the capital's ordinary machinery. In Kyiv, it listed traction substations and other rail infrastructure, an Auchan hypermarket and similar stores in the Obolon district, power substations across several districts, a trolleybus depot, and Zhuliany airport. In Kyiv Oblast, there are substations near Bucha and Irpin, many more that feed the railways, possible fuel depots near Borodianka and in the Bila Tserkva district, and the airfield at Vasylkiv. The account could not be independently verified. Jet-drone defenses run late Ukraine is racing to build a large-scale defense against jet-powered drones, the fast Gerans that have strained Kyiv's air cover, but the channel's administrator said the work was moving at "its own pace". "If we manage a proper counter before winter, that will be very lucky," he added. title: Year ago, only 12 Ukrainian brigades could order weapons online. Now, 500 units participate in revolutionary program that has delivered 1.3 million drones to front
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A year ago, 12 Ukrainian brigades could order their own weapons off a state marketplace. Now, more than 500 units can. DOT-Chain Defense, which lets frontline units order necessary supplies using state funds or bonuses with just a few clicks, has scaled across most of Ukraine's Defense Forces, the Defense Ministry said . The platform is the delivery backbone of Ukraine's soldier-led procurement revolution. It lies in a shift in the philosophy of defense procurement. Ukraine is abandoning the Soviet principle of "fight with whatever is handed down from above" and transitioning to a market-based model that centers on the choice of the individual soldier. Over its first year, it has put more than 1.3 million drones and other systems into units' hands, worth about $1.9 billion, and the orders show what this war runs on: 84 percent are drones, with electronic-warfare gear and ground robots making up most of the rest. It is also the engine behind the points-for-kills system that lets units bank credit for battlefield results and spend it on their own equipment. Access jumps from 12 to 500 units The growth has been steep. DOT-Chain Defense is now used by combat units across the armed forces, the National Guard, the border and special transport services, the police, the Security Service, and Defense Intelligence, says Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik. Assault regiments and the "Drone Line" project have joined, ordering unmanned systems to their own specifications. Drones dominate the orders By the ministry's count, electronic-warfare systems make up 8.6 percent of everything ordered, ground robotic complexes 7.2 percent, and ammunition a sliver at 0.2 percent. The gear, worth about $1.9 billion, came both through direct marketplace purchases and through the "Army of Drones. Bonus" program, the points system tied to the same platform. The US copies the model The approach has drawn imitators. The US has launched its own Amazon-style marketplace for military drones, explicitly modeled on Ukraine's Brave1 Market and DOT-Chain Defense. For Ukraine, the payoff is data: a running record of which weapons work on which part of the front, which the state uses to scale up what performs. title: He swore to defend Ukraine, then switched to Russia when it seized Crimea. Twelve years later, Ukrainian FPV drone found him commanding Russian regiment
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine has taken out a Russian artillery regiment commander in Kherson who was once a Ukrainian naval officer and who betrayed his country in 2014. Colonel Oleksandr Isaiev, a Mykolaiv native who defected to Russia during the seizure of Crimea and rose to command Russia's 8th Artillery Regiment, was killed by a Ukrainian FPV drone on 19 September, the Book of Executioners, a Ukrainian government project documenting Russian war crimes, said . Isaiev's death, if confirmed, closes a decade-long arc of betrayal. The Ukrainian citizen, who served in Ukraine's military from 1992, defected while serving as a senior officer in Ukraine's coastal artillery, joined Russia's Black Sea Fleet, and by 2024 was commanding a Russian regiment that shelled the country he had sworn to defend. A drone finds the commander The regiment Isaiev led, military unit 87714, operated on the coastal tactical axis in southern Ukraine as part of Russia's "Dnepr" grouping, the project said. An FPV drone, the small first-person-view aircraft that now dominates the front, struck him in Kherson Oblast on 19 September. The project provided no further details on the location, time, or circumstances of the strike. The betrayal dates to Crimea Isaiev was by 2014 chief of staff and first deputy commander of the 406th Separate Coastal Artillery Brigade in Ukraine's navy. When Russia seized Crimea that year, he switched sides, in what Ukraine calls high treason, and took a post as chief of staff and deputy commander of the same 8th Artillery Regiment on the Russian side. Discharged to the reserve in 2015, he returned to Russian service in October 2022 to join the war against Ukraine, and in September 2024 was made the regiment's commander and promoted to colonel. A database keeps the list The Book of Executioners is Ukraine's public register of those it accuses of crimes against the country, and it closed its report on Isaiev with a standing vow: every war crime will be investigated, every war criminal identified, found, and, in time, punished. title: CCA Builders Start Revving Production Rates, as They Await 2027 Funding
body: General Atomics Aeronautical Systems Inc. and Anduril Industries both say they’re ready to produce Collaborative Combat Aircraft in volume as they wait for a fiscal 2027 budget to fund that work. General Atomics announced earlier this week it has the capacity to produce its FQ-42A Vengeance drones at a rate of “six aircraft per month to meet USAF goals” and could make more if needed. Competitor Anduril, which started production of its FQ-44A Fury at its new Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio in March, aims to build 150 aircraft annually, its officials said last week at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference. The Air Force’s 2027 budget request includes $996.5 million to acquire production CCAs in fiscal 2027, plus another $150 million in advance procurement funds for 2028. But USAF has not specified how many aircraft that might cover. General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley declined to tell Air & Space Forces Magazine exactly how many FQ-42s are rolling off the company’s production line right now, but did confirm production is underway. “Some of those aircraft will become company aircraft,” he said, meaning that not all are for its Air Force customer. Brinkley said the company’s potential production expansion could be used to answer international demand for its Gambit series of autonomous drones, which are closely related to the FQ-42. General Atomics also said in its statement that it is self-funding FQ-42 production today as it awaits Congressional fiscal 2027 appropriations. The new fiscal year launches Oct. 1, but lawmakers failed to pass a budget for fiscal ’27, and instead passed a continuing resolution that would hold current year funding steady, but provides no new funding. The measure ensures funding through Dec. 11, 2026. GA’s self-funding will help support the government’s procurement plans and prevent delivery delays, the company said, and building aircraft for its own fleet will help it invest in new technologies that reduce risk and increase capabilities. The Air Force plans to use CCAs as a complement to crewed fighters in a bid to add combat capacity at a lower cost than convention fighter jets. CCAs are designed to be flown semi-autonomously, at times alongside piloted fighters like the F-22 and F-35 Lightning II, and could eventually carry out a variety of missions including air-to-air or air-to-ground strikes; intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance; or electronic warfare operations. The concept is still comparatively early in its development. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 that USAF is aiming to field at least 500 CCAs by 2032. The Anduril and General Atomics CCAs were selected following a competition in April 2024, andboth companies won initial production contracts in June 2026. General Atomics said a new FQ-42 was delivered to Creech Air Force Base, Nev., on Sept. 18, for test and evaluation. Creech is home to the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit, which has been experimenting with CCAs to develop approaches to how they might be employed in real-life operations. Jason Levin, Anduril’s senior vice president for air dominance and strike, said Sept. 14 that his firm delivered an FQ-44 to the EOU in August. Prior to that, the YFQ-44A prototype took part in two exercises with the EOU, the first in April and the second in July. The July exercise at Creech, Levin said, demonstrated that CCA had advanced enough for a single Air Force operator to launch and recover an aircraft on his own after just a few hours of training. “The Air Force was operating mission autonomy by themselves, which was a first,” Levin said. “They were flying multiple times a day, operating mission autonomy without Anduril personnel—they were on-site kind of helping, but it was really the Air Force operating that.” Levin said that during the July exercise, Fury flew in the same airspace as crewed fighters and other drones using mission autonomy, helping build Airmen’s trust that CCAs can operate in congested airspace. The production model of the FQ-44 that will start to roll off the line next year at Arsenal-1 will be able to carry four air-to-air weapons, such as the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, under its wings. The FQ-42, General Atomics said, has flown in formation with piloted F-35 Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle jets to prepare for future test flights, when fighter pilots will actually command the drones. The FQ-42 represents fifth-generation stealth and operates with an internal weapons bay. General Atomics previously conducted flights of its MQ-20 Avenger drone, operating as a CCA surrogate, to demonstrate how collaborative control flights might work. The company said its aircraft, including the Vengeance, Avenger, and XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station, have flown both semi-autonomously and autonomously using AI pilots and under the collaborative control of human pilots flying in the F-22 Raptor and F-35. “The CCA program’s rate of progress has been incredible,” said Mike Atwood, vice president of advanced programs at General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, in a company statement. “Every week, the Air Force is pushing forward with new and more impressive accomplishments using Vengeance. It’s amazing to think of how far this program has come in such a short amount of time.” The post CCA Builders Start Revving Production Rates, as They Await 2027 Funding appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: “Food must never be used as a weapon”: EU calls for Black Sea attack moratorium
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas called for a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea to restore safe navigation and allow Ukraine's grain exports to reach global markets. She made the call at a UN General Assembly side event co-chaired with the foreign ministers of France, Romania, and Ukraine on 22 September in New York. Since June, Russia has systematically struck Ukrainian ports, grain terminals, and commercial cargo ships in the Black Sea, killing crew members and crippling the export corridor that carries the bulk of Ukraine's agricultural output. The campaign—part of Russia's broader war, now in its fifth year—has disrupted global food supply chains and pushed the Black Sea toward a crisis the EU warned could surpass the 2022 grain-price shock. Kallas said Black Sea exports have effectively ground to a halt since August because Russian attacks made commercial shipping unviable. The Gulf conflict and climate change are adding further pressure, she said. Ukraine supplies 15% of global corn exports, 10% of wheat, 15–20% of barley, and about 50% of sunflower oil, with around 90% moving through the Black Sea corridor, Kallas said . Egypt, the world's largest wheat importer, has shifted some purchases away from Russia and Ukraine as costs have risen. "Food must never be used as a weapon in the Black Sea or anywhere else," Kallas said. "Wars make affordable food disappear from dinner tables of millions of people around the globe." Kallas called the proposal a new "Black Sea grain arrangement," separate from the Black Sea Grain Initiative , a 2022 deal brokered by Türkiye and the United Nations that Russia left in July 2023. She said the 2022 grain-price surge showed the strategic importance of the Black Sea for global security, international trade, energy, and food security. She called on the international community to ensure safe passage of civilian vessels, protect critical infrastructure, and restore the trade route. If Russia simply stopped its attacks in the Black Sea, farmers, traders, and international food markets would have the predictability they need at this critical moment, she said. In 2025 alone, the EU mobilized €2.1 billion to strengthen global food security, Kallas added, and the EU Solidarity Lanes have facilitated about €304 billion in trade since May 2022. At a press stakeout on 23 September, Kallas said the EU was "particularly concerned by the attacks in the Black Sea" and that "Russia is trying to choke off Ukrainian grain exports, thus jeopardizing global food security." Russia has not publicly responded to Kallas's call. In August, Moscow dismissed a similar proposal relayed by Türkiye, with Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova stating it saw no grounds for measures that would give Kyiv a "temporary reprieve." A summer of strikes Russia intensified strikes on Ukrainian ports and commercial shipping in June and July. Those strikes cut Ukrainian deepwater terminal capacity from roughly 7 million to 4–5 million metric tons per month, according to Barva Invest analyst Bohdan Kostetskyi. Ukrainian forces, in turn, struck Russia's grain terminals at Novorossiysk and Taman. Those strikes and the suspension of navigation in the Sea of Azov since July took more than 90% of Russia's Azov–Black Sea grain export capacity offline by mid-August. Russia kills captain of Tanzanian-flagged ship in latest attack on civilian shipping in Black Sea The cost of sailing The Lloyd's of London Joint War Committee has extended its high-risk designation to the entire Black Sea, pushing war-risk insurance premiums to hundreds of thousands of dollars per voyage. Alternative routes through the Danube have partly compensated, but shipping from Ukraine to Egypt has taken 26–33 days, more than twice as long as before. Russian Black Sea attacks, low Danube waters push EU to seek alternative routes for Ukrainian grain exports For Ukraine, restoring safer navigation would reopen its largest agricultural export route, reduce reliance on slower and more expensive alternatives, and help exporters move the harvest and earn foreign currency. The attacks have not stopped. Overnight on 23 September, Russia struck a cargo ship under an Antigua and Barbuda flag in the Black Sea, killing its captain, a Ukrainian citizen, Ukraine's sea ports administration said. The Navy evacuated the crew and put out the fire. title: Russia strikes Kyiv with ballistic and hypersonic missiles, damaging maternity hospital amid US-led push for energy truce
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russia's large combined missile-and-drone attack on Kyiv early on 24 September killed two people in the capital and damaged residential and civilian infrastructure, including a maternity hospital, according to Vitali Klitschko, the capital's mayor. The strike involved 282 attack drones alongside ballistic and hypersonic missiles, Ukraine's Air Force said . The strike came as US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy were pursuing an energy ceasefire during the UN General Assembly in New York. Ukraine was ready to stop attacks on Russian energy facilities if Moscow agreed to stop striking Ukraine's energy system, Zelenskyy said after meeting Trump on 22 September. Air defense intercepts over 200 targets Russia launched Zircon hypersonic missiles, an unspecified number of Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles, and 282 Shahed-type and Gerbera attack drones, Ukraine's Air Force said. The drones were accompanied by Banderol and Dan-T loitering munitions, as well as parody decoy drones. By 08:00, Ukrainian forces had destroyed or suppressed 227 targets, including four Zircons, three ballistic missiles, one Banderol/Dan-T loitering munition, and 219 drones. The Air Force did not disclose how many ballistic missiles Russia launched at Kyiv. Zelenskyy later said Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 60% of the ballistic missiles targeting the capital during three waves of attacks. Burned-out vehicles in a residential area of Kyiv after Russia's missile strike on 24 September 2026. Photo: State Emergency Service of Kyiv Zelenskyy added that the ballistic attack came while he was meeting US lawmakers in New York to discuss sanctions against Russia. He also called for more ballistic missile interceptors, saying Russia had targeted civilian infrastructure, residential buildings, a maternity hospital, energy facilities, and logistics. Maternity hospital, residential buildings damaged In Kyiv's Podilsky district, the maternity hospital's windows and part of its facade were damaged, according to the Ministry of Health. No casualties were reported inside the facility. One person was killed in a nearby parking lot, and a clinic-diagnostic center was also damaged. In Dniprovskyi district, a residential building, a non-residential building, and several private houses were damaged. One private house was partially destroyed. A three-story administrative building was also damaged, and a body was found there. In the Solomiansky district, a warehouse was partially destroyed and caught fire. Missile debris fell on a roadway in Darnytskyi district. A firefighter works amid burning debris in Kyiv after Russia's combined missile-and-drone attack on 24 September 2026. Photo: State Emergency Service of Kyiv In Kyiv Oblast, one person was injured, and eight objects were damaged across three districts, the Kyiv Oblast Military Administration said . The damage included private houses and vehicles. Zelenskyy called for stronger sanctions against Russia and more air-defense interceptors as the attacks continued during the UN General Assembly week. title: Russian Strike Damages Orthodox Church in Kramatorsk, Ukraine
body: A Russian aerial strike has severely damaged an Orthodox church in the Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk, with images showing extensive destruction to the building’s roof, walls and dome. Orthodox church damaged in Russian strike in Ukraine A Russian aerial strike has severely damaged the Church of St. John the Baptist in Kramatorsk, Donetsk Oblast. Video shows the aftermath, with major damage visible to the church’s walls, roof and dome, while debris… pic.twitter.com/THrhHD0TbJ — Greek City Times (@greekcitytimes) September 24, 2026 The Church of St. John the Baptist , which belongs to the Ukrainian Orthodox Church, was damaged during Russian shelling on September 22, according to the Ukrainian Orthodox Church’s press service. Photographs released after the attack show debris scattered across the church grounds, while sections of the building’s metal framework appear twisted by the force of the blast. The roof and dome have also sustained significant damage. The Ukrainian Orthodox Church reported the destruction following the strike, while Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Russian forces dropped an aerial bomb on residential areas of Kramatorsk on the evening of September 22. According to the emergency service, the attack damaged 10 apartment buildings, the church and a car . It was not immediately clear whether anyone was killed or injured in the vicinity of the church. Kramatorsk repeatedly targeted The latest strike came only days after another Russian air attack on Kramatorsk. On September 20, an airstrike caused a fire covering approximately 4,800 square metres at a two storey educational facility. Two people were reported injured. Earlier attacks involving guided aerial bombs also killed a woman and injured a man in the city. Kramatorsk, in Donetsk Oblast, has remained a frequent target during Russia’s full scale invasion of Ukraine. The damage to the Church of St. John the Baptist adds another religious site to the growing list of Ukrainian churches and historic places of worship damaged or destroyed during the war. Source: NV English, Ukrainian Orthodox Church and Ukraine’s State Emergency Service The post Russian Strike Damages Orthodox Church in Kramatorsk, Ukraine appeared first on Greek City Times .

title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1673: Ukraine’s two steel plants, which produce 70% of country’s steel, are buckling under Russian strikes
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Exclusive Two plants make 70% of Ukraine's steel. Russia hit both. Then ports closed, rail costs rose 30%, and the EU's carbon tax kicked in . The head of Ukraine's largest steel plant says the government needs a single rescue document with deadlines and assigned agencies, because each problem stalls when handled alone. title: Russia may target southern Europe with drones launched from merchant ships—El Mundo
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); US intelligence has warned Spain, France, and Italy that Russia may be preparing to launch drones at one of them from merchant ships in the Mediterranean, El Mundo reported on 23 September, citing sources familiar with the alert. Neither the CIA nor the three governments have confirmed it. Russia has intensified a campaign of sabotage, airspace incursions, and other provocations against European states supporting Ukraine while keeping its actions below the threshold of open conflict with NATO. A maritime drone attack would extend that campaign into southern Europe, turning the Mediterranean into a launch zone for deniable strikes on civilian or military infrastructure. El Mundo based its account on a source close to Lithuania's Defense Ministry and analysts familiar with a CIA report circulated among European foreign ministries. The reported plan would hide small Russian Gerbera drones inside shipping containers aboard merchant ships and launch them from the Mediterranean. According to El Mundo, a Gerbera drone can travel up to 600 kilometers depending on payload and wind, potentially putting targets along NATO's southern coast within reach of a ship offshore. The Gerbera drone's reported 4–5 kilogram explosive payload would be unlikely to destroy a large facility, the newspaper said, but could start a fire, damage exposed equipment, or temporarily close an airport or port. All three countries hold elections in 2027 and have political forces capable of exploiting fear and fatigue with Ukraine, with connections to Kremlin interests especially visible in France and Italy, El Mundo reported. Keir Giles, a British defense analyst, said frontline states are not necessarily the targets—the target will be wherever Europe's weakest point is, naming the UK and Spain as countries that have not invested in air and missile defense adequate to the Russian threat. Explosives found meters from the drone that crashed near a Bundeswehr air base—investigators say it matches the GRU’s Leipzig attack devices El Mundo placed the warning alongside earlier Russian drone incidents on NATO territory. In September 2025, 19 unarmed drones strayed into Polish airspace. German authorities later attributed an explosive-carrying drone incident at Leipzig airport to Russia. The war has reached Mediterranean shipping Russia's oil shipments and naval presence, alongside reported Ukrainian operations, have brought the conflict into the region in several ways. A source cited by Ukrainian media said Ukraine's Security Service struck a Russian shadow-fleet tanker there in December 2025. Such vessels carry Russian oil outside Western sanctions, making the sea a route for Moscow's war revenue and a target for Kyiv. The French outlet RFI later reported that Ukraine may have established a drone launch site in Libya for strikes on Russian shipping. Kyiv has not confirmed the reported site. Russia's military position in the region has also shifted. British intelligence assessed in January 2025 that its Mediterranean naval force lacked access to its Syrian base at Tartus after Bashar al-Assad's fall.
